paper.title: HIGHT: A New Block Cipher Suitable for Low-Resource Device

program.how: written for ounce-core from the algorithm description; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: 9 distinct single-block ECB known-answer vectors match (9 of 9)
8 CBC vectors match (8 of 8; one or two blocks)
44 CTR vectors match (44 of 44; these are successive prefixes of one keystream, so they are not 44 independent tests)

expected_values_source.what: the Crypto++ test-vector file hight.txt, whose three sections cite the KISA HIGHT reference code files KISA_HIGHT_ECB.c, KISA_HIGHT_CBC.c and KISA_HIGHT_CTR.c (exact duplicates inside the file were removed: 15 ECB entries hold 9 distinct vectors). Byte order: key[i] = MK_i, plaintext[i] = P_i, ciphertext[i] = C_i, the array order of those files, fixed by the first vector and then applied unchanged
expected_values_source.note: the HIGHT paper's own printed test vector was not fetched and is not checked here; the vectors are the KISA reference outputs as relayed by Crypto++. Data copied as numbers; no code was copied

negative_control: built with HIGHT_DELTA0=0x5b (first LFSR constant 0x5b instead of 0x5a), 0 of 9 ECB, 0 of 8 CBC and 0 of 44 CTR vectors match, program exits 1
not_checked: security claims, hardware gate counts or throughput figures
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about the authors' hardware)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces the KISA reference HIGHT ciphertexts for 61 inputs. It does not show the cipher is secure.
